concepts.title: Framing a regression question
concepts.outcome: Name the response, the predictor or predictors, and say whether the relationship is statistical rather than exact.

keyPoints.text: Regression relates a response (the outcome you want to understand or predict) to one or more predictors. Older texts also call them dependent and independent variables.

Regression studies statistical relationships: there is a trend, but individual points scatter around it. An exact formula, like Celsius to Fahrenheit, is a deterministic relationship and needs no regression.

concepts.title: The linear regression model
concepts.outcome: Explain that the model describes the mean response as a straight-line function of the predictors.

keyPoints.text: Simple linear regression has one predictor; multiple linear regression has two or more. Both summarise the trend between the predictors and a quantitative response.
Fitting a line answers one question: which straight line best summarises the trend between two quantitative variables?
keyPoints.locator: 1.2 What is the Best Fitting Line?

anchor.end: what is the best fitting line

concepts.title: Population line versus estimated line
concepts.outcome: Distinguish the unknown population regression line from the line estimated from a sample.

keyPoints.text: The population regression line describes how the mean response changes with x across the whole population. Its intercept and slope are unknown parameters.
We almost never observe the whole population, so we estimate the population line from a sample. The fitted intercept and slope are estimates that would change with a different sample.

concepts.title: Least squares
concepts.outcome: Explain how least squares chooses the line, and what a residual (prediction error) is.

keyPoints.text: A prediction error (residual) is the gap between an observed response and the line's prediction for it. Least squares picks the line that makes the sum of the squared prediction errors as small as possible.
keyPoints.locator: 1.2 What is the Best Fitting Line?

keyPoints.text: Formulas give the least squares intercept and slope directly, so no search over candidate lines is needed. The result is called the least squares regression line.
keyPoints.locator: 1.2 What is the Best Fitting Line?

concepts.title: Interpreting the slope and intercept
concepts.outcome: Interpret a fitted slope and intercept in the units of the data, and recognise when the intercept has no meaning.

keyPoints.text: The slope is the change in the mean response for each one-unit increase in the predictor.
keyPoints.locator: 1.2 What is the Best Fitting Line?

keyPoints.text: The intercept is the predicted mean response when x is 0, which only means something if x = 0 lies within the range of the data. Predicting outside that range is extrapolation and can be nonsense.
keyPoints.locator: 1.2 What is the Best Fitting Line?

concepts.title: Error variance and the residual standard error
concepts.outcome: Explain what the mean square error and the residual standard error estimate.

keyPoints.text: The mean square error (MSE) estimates the common variance of the responses around the population line, that is, how much points scatter around the true trend.
keyPoints.locator: 1.4 What is The Common Error Variance?

keyPoints.text: The square root of the MSE, often written S, is the regression or residual standard error: the typical size of a prediction error, in the response's own units.
keyPoints.locator: 1.4 What is The Common Error Variance?

concepts.title: R-squared
concepts.outcome: Interpret R-squared as the share of variation in the response accounted for by the model, and know its limits.

keyPoints.text: R-squared is the percentage of the variation in the response that is reduced by taking the predictor into account.
R-squared and the correlation coefficient can both be swung by a single data point, or a few, so a summary number never replaces looking at the plot.

misconceptions.claim: A large R-squared means the straight line fits the data well.
misconceptions.correction: A large R-squared only says the line accounts for much of the variation. Another shape, such as a curve, may describe the data better; check the plot.

misconceptions.claim: An R-squared near 0 means x and y are unrelated.
misconceptions.correction: R-squared measures linear association only. It can be 0 even when x and y have a perfect curved relationship.

concepts.title: Association is not causation
concepts.outcome: Explain why a strong regression relationship does not show that the predictor causes the response.

keyPoints.text: A large R-squared does not mean x causes the changes in y. Saying x 'explains' the variation is fine only if that is not read as cause.

anchor.end: x causes the changes in y

keyPoints.text: Two variables can be strongly associated across a dataset without one causing the other, as in Penn State's example of wine consumption and heart-disease deaths across countries.

concepts.title: Multiple linear regression
concepts.outcome: Extend the model to several predictors and interpret each slope with the others held constant.

keyPoints.text: Multiple linear regression extends the simple model from one predictor to two or more.
Each slope is the change in the mean response per unit increase in its predictor while all the other predictors are held constant.

anchor.start: per unit increase in the associated

keyPoints.text: The same model checks still apply, but the error distribution is now considered at a fixed set of values for all the predictors rather than one.

concepts.title: Inference about a slope
concepts.outcome: Test whether a population slope is zero, and read a confidence interval for it.

keyPoints.text: Asking whether x is linearly related to y becomes a test of whether the population slope is 0. A t-test for the slope answers it; in simple regression an ANOVA F-test is an alternative.
If a confidence interval for the slope contains 0, the data give no evidence of a linear relationship in the population. If it excludes 0, they do.
keyPoints.locator: 2.1 Inference for the Population Intercept and Slope

concepts.title: The overall F-test
concepts.outcome: Use the overall F-test to ask whether a model with several predictors is useful at all, and tell it apart from tests of one slope or a subset.

keyPoints.text: Multiple regression supports three different tests: that one slope is 0, that all slopes are 0, and that a subset of slopes is 0. Each answers a different research question.
Asking whether a model with at least one predictor is useful means testing that all the slope parameters are zero, which is the analysis of variance F-test.

concepts.title: Confidence versus prediction intervals
concepts.outcome: Choose between an interval for the mean response and an interval for a single new response, and explain why one is wider.
aliases: confidence interval for the mean response

keyPoints.text: A confidence interval estimates the mean response at a given x. A prediction interval covers one new response at that x.
A prediction interval is wider because its standard error adds an extra term for a single response's own scatter around the mean, which the standard error of the fit does not include.
keyPoints.locator: 3.3 Prediction Interval for a New Response

keyPoints.text: Both intervals are narrowest at the mean of the predictor values and widen further out.

misconceptions.claim: A 95% confidence interval for the mean response shows where 95% of new individual observations will fall.
misconceptions.correction: That is what a prediction interval is for. The confidence interval is about the mean response and is always narrower.

concepts.title: The model's assumptions
concepts.outcome: State the four LINE conditions and say what each requires.

keyPoints.text: The simple linear regression model rests on four conditions, LINE: the mean response is a Linear function of x, and the errors are Independent, Normally distributed and of Equal variance at each x.
All four can be stated at once: the errors are independent normal random variables with mean zero and constant variance.

misconceptions.claim: Linear regression requires the predictors and the response to be normally distributed.
misconceptions.correction: The normality condition is about the errors at each value of the predictors, not about the raw x or y values.

concepts.title: Residual diagnostics
concepts.outcome: Use residual plots to check the model's conditions and spot problems.

keyPoints.text: A residuals-versus-fits plot (residuals against fitted values) is the most common check. It reveals non-linearity, unequal error variances and outliers.
A residuals-versus-order plot checks independence by revealing serial correlation, but only when you know the order the data were collected in.

anchor.end: in which the data were collected

keyPoints.text: A normal probability plot of the residuals checks the normality condition: if the errors are normal, the plot is roughly a straight line.

concepts.title: Categorical predictors
concepts.outcome: Code a categorical predictor with indicator variables and interpret the result against a baseline group.

keyPoints.text: A categorical predictor enters the model through 0/1 indicator variables: 1 for observations in a group, 0 for the rest.
A categorical variable with c groups needs c - 1 indicator variables. The group left out becomes the baseline the others are compared with.

misconceptions.claim: Create one indicator variable for every category.
misconceptions.correction: With an intercept in the model, c categories need only c - 1 indicators. One for every category adds a redundant variable the model cannot separate from the intercept.

concepts.title: Interactions
concepts.outcome: Recognise when the effect of one predictor depends on another, and interpret a model with an interaction term.

keyPoints.text: Two predictors interact when the effect of one on the response depends on the value of the other.

anchor.end: on the value of the other

keyPoints.text: Once an interaction is in the model, a slope can no longer be read as the change in the mean response for a one-unit increase in that predictor alone.

keyPoints.text: If an interaction term stays in the model, its main effects stay too, whether or not they are significant. This is the hierarchy principle.

concepts.title: Polynomial terms
concepts.outcome: Add polynomial terms to capture curvature while staying within linear regression.

keyPoints.text: When residual plots show curvature, adding powers of a predictor (squared, cubed and so on) can capture a nonlinear relationship.

anchor.start: One way to try to account

keyPoints.text: Polynomial regression is still linear regression, because the model is linear in its coefficients even when it is curved in x.

misconceptions.claim: Linear regression can only fit straight lines.
misconceptions.correction: "Linear" means linear in the coefficients. Polynomial and other transformed terms let a linear regression fit curves.

concepts.title: Transformations
concepts.outcome: Choose a transformation of the response or predictors to fix curvature or unequal variance, and interpret the result.

keyPoints.text: When the error variances are unequal, transforming the response and/or the predictors (or using weighted least squares) can fix it.

anchor.start: If there are unequal error variances

keyPoints.text: Taking the logarithm of the response is one way to model a nonlinear relationship between the response and the predictors.

concepts.title: Multicollinearity
concepts.outcome: Recognise strongly related predictors, explain what they do to coefficient estimates, detect them with VIF, and know how to reduce them.

keyPoints.text: When predictors are strongly related, each coefficient depends on which other predictors are in the model, and the coefficients become less precise as more are added.
Warning signs include coefficients that change from model to model, and individual t-tests that are not significant while the overall F-test is.
keyPoints.locator: 12.4 Detecting Multicollinearity Using Variance Inflation Factors

keyPoints.text: A variance inflation factor (VIF) measures how much the variance of an estimated coefficient is inflated by its predictor's relationship with the others.
keyPoints.locator: 12.4 Detecting Multicollinearity Using Variance Inflation Factors

anchor.end: how much the variance is inflated

keyPoints.text: To reduce multicollinearity that comes from the data, remove one or more of the offending predictors, or collect more data under different conditions.

anchor.start: the previous section illustrated, one way

misconceptions.claim: VIF analysis is a remedy that removes multicollinearity.
misconceptions.correction: VIF only detects and measures multicollinearity. Reducing it means changing the model or the data, for example by removing a predictor or collecting more data.

concepts.title: Outliers, leverage and influence
concepts.outcome: Tell outliers from high-leverage points, and judge whether either actually changes the fitted model.

keyPoints.text: An outlier is an observation whose response is very different from what the model predicts for it.

anchor.start: If an observation has a response

keyPoints.text: A high-leverage point has an unusual combination of predictor values. Outliers and high-leverage points are different, and one point can be both.

anchor.end: an outlier and have high leverage

keyPoints.text: Being unusual is not enough to matter: the question is whether a point has undue influence, meaning it actually changes the fitted model.

concepts.title: Choosing predictors
concepts.outcome: Explain the costs of leaving out or adding the wrong predictors, and use a model-building strategy rather than a mechanical search alone.

keyPoints.text: Leaving out an important predictor (an underspecified model) is the worst case: coefficients and predictions are biased, and confidence intervals are wider than they should be.

concepts.title: Hold-out (test) error
concepts.outcome: Estimate how a model will perform on new data by evaluating it on data it was not trained on.

keyPoints.text: Testing a model on the data it was trained on is a methodological mistake: a model that memorised that data would score perfectly yet predict nothing useful. This is overfitting.

keyPoints.text: To avoid it, part of the data is held out as a test set and used only to evaluate the model.

concepts.title: Cross-validation
concepts.outcome: Use k-fold cross-validation to estimate test error without setting aside a single fixed validation set.

keyPoints.text: In k-fold cross-validation the training data are split into k folds. Each fold in turn is used to validate a model trained on the other k - 1.
The reported score is the average over the k folds. It costs more computation, but wastes less data than holding out one fixed validation set.

concepts.title: Overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off
concepts.outcome: Explain why a more complex model can fit the training data better yet predict new data worse.

keyPoints.text: Adding unimportant predictors, transformations and interactions makes a model more complicated and can overfit it, increasing uncertainty about the effects that matter.

keyPoints.text: Training error is easy to compute but can dramatically underestimate the error on new observations, which is what matters for prediction.

keyPoints.text: Searching a very large space of candidate models can overfit and give coefficient estimates with high variance.

misconceptions.claim: A model that fits the training data better will predict new data better.
misconceptions.correction: Training error keeps falling as a model gets more complex, but error on new data eventually rises. Judge models on held-out data.

prerequisites.reason: A model needs a response and predictors before it can relate them.
Least squares is how the line's coefficients are chosen.
A slope can only be interpreted once the model it belongs to is understood.
Multiple regression extends the one-predictor model.
R-squared compares the least squares residuals with the total variation.
The error variance is estimated from the least squares residuals.
The normal equations solve the least squares problem directly.
Gradient descent minimises the same least squares cost iteratively.
Residual plots check the assumptions, so the assumptions come first.
Inference is about the population slope that the sample slope estimates.
The overall F-test asks whether a multi-predictor model is useful at all.
Indicator variables enter the model as extra predictors.
An interaction is defined between two predictors in the same model.
Collinearity is a relationship among several predictors.
Cross-validation repeats the hold-out idea across folds.
